newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania to restructure state-run Tarom airline.
newsitem.headline: Romania to restructure state-run Tarom airline.

text.p: Romania's transport ministry pledged on Wednesday to proceed with plans to restructure state airline Tarom SA and said it had won the agreement of reluctant trade unions.
"Nothing and nobody can stop us from restructuring Tarom. The programme is up and running," ministry State Secretary Aleodor Francu told Reuters.

Under the plan, Tarom would undergo a rapid restructuring, including layoffs and sale of its outdated Soviet-made Ilyushin-62, IL-18 and Tupolev-154 aircraft or their redeployment in a new company. Some staff involved in their maintenance would be laid off and others retrained.
Francu said the project had been agreed in principle with trade unions, which threatened this week to go on strike and ground flights unless the ministry revised its plans.
"We had extensive talks with the trade unions yesterday and we managed to reach an agreement," he said.
Romania's flag carrier faces serious financial problems. Its internal debts total 80 billion lei ($11.1 million) and external debts $15.5 million, according to local media reports.
The unions accused the ministry of turning a blind eye to monopolistic practices of private companies operating catering, handling and fuelling services.
"The ministry will deal with this issue, too. There are several companies interested in getting part of the operation so we will create competition in the sector," Francu said.
He said the ministry would re-evaluate Tarom's regular flight routes before deciding on the layoffs.
"We plan to use some of the Soviet-made planes to create a new company, for cargo transport or chartered flights," he said.
"Romania doesn't have a strong air market to ensure a minimum of 2,000 hours of flight per year for each plane, so we will have to look elsewhere."
Tarom sources said the airline was clinching space-sharing cargo accords with other airlines, with plans to turn Bucharest's Otopeni airport into a cargo hub for Eastern Europe.

Francu also said he was confident the new centrist government would support Tarom's plans to buy eight Boeing Next Generation 737s. The project was suspended last month when the finance ministry failed to guarantee the planned purchase.
Tarom's General Manager Dan Vulcan is expected to have talks on a cooperation accord with Trans-World Airlines of the United States in London this week.
Tarom's international routes are served by two A-310 Airbus planes, five Boeing 737s and six BAC 1-11 aircraft.
